headline.statement: The paper's stated purpose and its Conclusions are a head-to-head comparison of Cortexin, Cerebrolysin and Actovegin, but every statistical test it reports compares a drug against placebo or against intact controls -- no drug-versus-drug comparison appears anywhere in the paper.
headline.evidence: Aim: "This study was the first performed to compare the neuroprotective activity of Cerebrolysin, Actovegin and Cortexin in rodent models of acute and chronic brain ischemia." Conclusions: "Cortexin (1 or 3 mg/kg) as well as Cerebrolysin (538 or 1614 mg/kg) were comparable effective in models acute and chronic brain ischemia in rats." Every reported test carries one of two reference marks and no others -- Table 1 footnotes: "#-p <0.05 compared to Intact" and "*-p <0.05 compared to placebo (Kruskal-Wallis rank analysis and the Dunn post-hoc test)" -- and the captions of Figs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12 repeat the same two marks verbatim. At least five comparative statements are made in the text ("Actovegin showed inferiority to other drugs"; "in the group receiving Cortexin, unlike Cerebrolysin, the efficacy did not depend on the dose administered"; "Cerebrolysin had a similar pronounced and complex neuroprotective effects"; "while Actovegin was inferior to the other drugs"; and the Conclusions sentence above) with no supporting between-drug test statistic, p-value or interval.
headline.plain: The whole point of this study was to compare three brain drugs against each other, and its final conclusion says two of them worked equally well. But every statistical test the paper actually ran compared one drug against an untreated or placebo group -- never against another drug. Showing that two treatments each beat a placebo does not show that they match each other, and the paper contains no test or margin of error that would let a reader judge how different they might really be.

findings.title: Comparative conclusion drawn from separate placebo comparisons, with no drug-versus-drug test
findings.location: Conclusions; Abstract; Discussion; Results 3.2.1, 3.5.2, 3.6.1; Table 1 footnotes and captions of Figs 3-12
findings.reported: Conclusions: "Cortexin (1 or 3 mg/kg) as well as Cerebrolysin (538 or 1614 mg/kg) were comparable effective in models acute and chronic brain ischemia in rats." Aim: "the first performed to compare the neuroprotective activity of Cerebrolysin, Actovegin and Cortexin". Reference marks throughout: "#-p <0.05 compared to Intact; *-p <0.05 compared to placebo".
findings.computed: The absence-of-evidence check could not be run at all: it requires an interval estimate, and no confidence interval is reported for any outcome anywhere in the paper. No smallest effect size of interest is stated. The comparability claim is therefore inferred from both drugs separately reaching p<0.05 against a common comparator -- the difference-in-significance fallacy (Gelman & Stern 2006), which does not license a conclusion about the difference between them. The largest true Cortexin-versus-Cerebrolysin difference the data still permit cannot be bounded from anything printed.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The finding rests entirely on the paper's own footnotes, which state what each test compares, and on the absence of any interval estimate in the text, table, or supplements.

consequence.explanation: The Conclusions' central claim that Cortexin and Cerebrolysin are 'comparable effective', plus four further comparative statements ranking Actovegin below the other two and comparing Cortexin's dose-response to Cerebrolysin's, rest on an inference the reported analyses do not support.

findings.plain: The paper concludes that two of the drugs are equally effective and that a third is worse. To support a claim like that you have to compare the drugs directly. This paper never does: it compares each drug to a placebo group, finds several of them beat placebo, and infers from that pattern that they are similar to each other. That inference is not valid, and because the paper reports no margins of error anywhere, a reader cannot even work out how big a real difference between the drugs might still be hiding in the data.

findings.title: 'p <0.05' attached to a statement that two drug groups were comparable
findings.reported: "In animals treated with Cerebrolysin at a dose of 1614 mg/kg/day, most of the indicators were comparable to those obtained in animals treated with Cortexin at a dose of 3 mg/kg/day (p <0.05)." Two sentences earlier, the same paragraph uses the opposite convention for a similarity claim: "the average values of most indicators (except for the lactate content) did not statistically significantly differ from those of intact (p> 0.05 in each case)".
findings.computed: Read as written, p<0.05 indicates a statistically significant difference, which contradicts the word 'comparable' in the same clause. The paragraph applies p>0.05 correctly to a no-difference claim about a different contrast, so the two conventions are used inconsistently within a single paragraph. No test statistic accompanies either statement, so the intended reading cannot be recovered from the paper.
findings.assumptions: Assumes the conventional reading of p<0.05 as evidence of a difference at the paper's own stated threshold ("The differences were considered statistically significant at p <0.05"). A benign reading is available and is probably the likeliest: the authors may have meant that both groups were significantly better than placebo and therefore similar in effect -- which would make this the same inferential error as Finding 1 rather than a typographical one.

consequence.explanation: This is the only sentence in the paper that puts a p-value on a Cortexin-versus-Cerebrolysin comparison, and as printed the p-value points the opposite way from the claim it supports.

findings.plain: In one sentence the authors say the two drugs produced comparable results, and then put a figure next to it that conventionally means the opposite -- that the two differed. In the same paragraph they use the correct notation for a genuine 'no difference' statement, so the two are inconsistent. This matters because it is the only place in the paper where any number is attached to a direct comparison between the two drugs.

findings.title: No test statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p-value, effect size or confidence interval anywhere in the paper
findings.location: Whole paper: Table 1 and its footnotes, the captions of Figs 3-14, and all of Results 3.1-3.9
findings.reported: Roughly thirty significance claims are made. Every one is reported as a threshold: "p <0.05", "p <0.001" or "p> 0.05". Methods 2.13: "The differences were considered statistically significant at p <0.05."
findings.computed: statcheck recovered zero NHST statistics from the entire 23-page article -- an accurate description of the reporting, not a tool failure. Separately, multiplicity_report over the 14-comparison Table 1 family returned n_tests = 0: all 14 were dropped rather than coerced, because every p is a bound rather than a value, so no family-wise or false-discovery correction can be computed and no surviving-claims interval can be quoted. Table 1 itself admits no arithmetic check either -- all 49 cells are median [Q1;Q3] on ordinal scales plus a bare n column, and GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require a mean and an SD.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Note in fairness that this is NOT uncorrected testing: Dunn's post-hoc test (nonparametric families) and the stated Bonferroni correction (ANOVA families) both do control multiplicity. The finding is that the reporting makes the correction impossible to verify, not that it is absent. Note also the mitigation: the raw participant-level data ARE deposited and were loaded here (12,201 numeric cells across 3 sheets), so a reader could in principle recompute everything -- the blackout is in the printed record, not in the underlying evidence.

consequence.explanation: Every significance claim in the paper, including all of those carried into the Abstract, is stated without a recomputable statistic.

findings.plain: The paper makes about thirty claims that a result was statistically significant, and for every one of them it prints only 'p less than 0.05' or 'p less than 0.001' -- never the underlying test result, the exact figure, the size of the effect, or a margin of error. Nothing in the paper's argument can therefore be re-derived by a reader from what is printed. The one saving grace is real and worth stating: the authors did deposit their raw animal-by-animal data in a public repository, and that file loads and is complete, so someone willing to redo the analysis from scratch could check the claims -- they just cannot check them from the article.

findings.title: Blinding of outcome assessment absent, and randomisation stated only for the 37-animal sub-experiment
findings.reported: The word 'randomly' appears once in the paper, for the 37-animal sub-study only: "an additional experiment was performed in limited number of animals (n = 37) randomly assigned to 4 groups". No allocation method is given for the 87-animal acute series or the 100-animal chronic series. No statement of blinding appears anywhere in the Methods, Results or Discussion (the only occurrence of 'blind' in the paper is "blindness of the animal", describing corneal protection during surgery).
findings.computed: The primary outcome in Table 1 is a pair of observer-rated ordinal scales -- the Garcia 18-point and Combs & D'Alecy 9-point scales, scored on "muscle tone, motor activity, basic physiological reflexes, coordination of movement, sensitivity to touch" and on "muscle strength, tenacity, traction and balance". The morphometric outcome in Figs 11-12 rests on an observer classifying neurons into three categories by appearance. Both are maximally susceptible to assessor expectancy, and neither is reported as blinded. The Discussion contains an explicit limitations section covering animal age, comorbidity, sex and the restricted necrosis sub-study, but does not mention blinding or allocation.
findings.assumptions: Assumes that a blinding or allocation procedure actually used but not reported would be a reporting omission rather than an absence -- the two are indistinguishable from the article. The judgement that this matters for these outcomes rests on the well-established preclinical finding that non-blinded and non-randomised animal stroke studies report substantially larger effects (Macleod / CAMARADES; the ARRIVE and STAIR reporting guidelines require both), which is an external benchmark I supply, not one the paper states.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the neurological-deficit result in Table 1, the hippocampal and cortical morphometry in Figs 11-12, and the behavioural battery -- all scored by human observers whose knowledge of group allocation is not excluded.

findings.plain: The main measurements here are human judgements: a scientist watches each rat and scores its reflexes and coordination, or looks down a microscope and sorts brain cells into 'normal', 'slightly damaged' and 'badly damaged'. The paper never says that the person doing the scoring was kept unaware of which drug each animal received, and it only describes randomly assigning animals to groups in one small side-experiment of 37 rats, not in the two main experiments of 87 and 100. In animal stroke research specifically, studies that omit these safeguards tend to report bigger benefits than studies that use them, so their absence is a reason to hold the size of the reported effects loosely.

findings.title: Mechanistic claim in the Abstract and Conclusions resting on duplicate (n = 2) receptor assays
findings.location: Fig 14 caption; Results 3.9; Abstract; Conclusions; S2 File
findings.reported: Fig 14 caption: "Cortexin receptor binding in vitro. Data shown as the median and range (n = 2)." Abstract and Results 3.9 report binding to AMPA-receptors (80.1%), kainate receptors (73.5%), mGluR1 (49.0%), GABAA1 (44.0%) and mGluR5 (39.7%). Conclusions: "Cortexin contains compounds acting on AMPA, kainate, mGluR1, GABAA1 and mGluR5 receptors in vitro".
findings.computed: With n = 2 the median is simply the midpoint of the two values and the 'range' is the pair itself, so the summary conveys no information the two raw numbers would not. The percentages are nevertheless carried into the Abstract to one decimal place, a precision duplicate assays cannot support. No dispersion beyond the pair, no replication, and no statistical test accompanies them. S2 File documents a 28-assay panel while the narrative names 5 targets -- the five highest -- and whether the remaining 23 appear in Fig 14 could not be determined because the figure was not read.
findings.assumptions: GRIM-percentage was deliberately NOT applied to these values: they are percent inhibition of radioligand binding, a continuous ratio, not a count out of a sample, and applying a granularity test would manufacture a false impossibility. The concern is statistical informativeness and selective emphasis, not arithmetic.

consequence.explanation: The Abstract's and the Conclusions' claim about how Cortexin works -- that it acts on AMPA, kainate, mGluR1, GABAA1 and mGluR5 receptors -- rests entirely on assays run twice each.

findings.plain: The paper's explanation of how the drug works comes from laboratory tests each run just twice. Two measurements cannot establish how variable a result is, yet the numbers are quoted to a tenth of a percent in the summary and the finding is repeated in the paper's final conclusion. The supplementary file also shows 28 different receptors were tested while only the five with the strongest response are named in the text, so a reader cannot see how the highlighted five compare with the rest.

findings.title: No mortality, exclusions or attrition reported across 184 surgically operated animals
findings.location: Methods 2.2 and 2.3; S1 File Table A; Discussion (limitations section)
findings.reported: Methods 2.2: "The study used 224 male albino rats (300-350 g)". S1 File Table A gives 18 group counts. The paper reports no deaths, no exclusions and no attrition at any point, and its limitations paragraph does not mention them.
findings.computed: The 18 group counts sum to exactly 224 (10+9+9+9+15+12+12+12+12+12+12+15+13+15+14+15+13+15 = 224, difference 0 at tolerance 0). Every animal stated to have been used therefore appears in an analysed group, leaving no room for losses and no way to tell whether 224 is the number obtained or the number analysed. 184 of the 224 underwent ischemia surgery (224 minus the three intact groups of 15, 10 and 15), including 87 rats given 90 minutes of filament middle cerebral artery occlusion followed by 10 days of survival. Final group sizes are uneven in a pattern that would be consistent with unreported losses from an intended 15 per group (chronic series: 15, 13, 15, 14, 15, 13, 15).
findings.assumptions: Rests on an external benchmark I supply, not one the paper states: filament MCAO with 90-minute occlusion carries appreciable mortality in the published literature (commonly reported in the 10-30% range at 24 h to 7 days), so zero losses across 87 such animals would be unusual. The paper states no expected or observed mortality, so this cannot be resolved from the text; an equally consistent reading is that 224 counts only the animals that completed the study.

consequence.explanation: Cannot be determined from the article: if animals were lost and their allocation was related to outcome, every group comparison would be affected, but the paper gives no basis for judging whether any were lost at all.

findings.plain: The paper says 224 rats were used, and the group sizes listed in the supplement add up to exactly 224 -- every animal is accounted for in an analysed group. But 184 of those rats had major surgery to block blood flow to the brain, a procedure that typically kills some proportion of animals, and the paper never mentions a single death, exclusion or dropout. It is impossible to tell from the article whether 224 is the number of rats the study started with or the number that survived to be analysed. If some animals were lost, knowing which groups they came from would matter for interpreting the results.

findings.title: Repeated measurements on the same animals analysed with between-groups tests only
findings.reported: Methods 2.13 lists only between-groups procedures: "Parametric data were compared using one-way analysis of variance (One-Way ANOVA) and t-student test with Bonferroni correction. Nonparametric data were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis rank analysis and the Dunn post-hoc test." No repeated-measures ANOVA, mixed model, Friedman test or within-animal adjustment is mentioned anywhere.
findings.computed: The design is repeatedly groups-by-time: Table 1 scores the same 87 rats at 3 h, 24 h and 10 days; Fig 7 follows the same animals across four training days; Fig 8 follows them across three treatment periods; Figs 5B and 6C measure the chronic-ischemia animals before and after treatment. At least one explicitly within-animal claim is made -- "After 10 days of treatment, the performance of animals receiving placebo in this test did not change significantly" (Results 3.3.1, chronic) -- and the Methods list no paired or repeated-measures test that could produce it.
findings.assumptions: A material counter-consideration applies and cannot be resolved from the paper: every reference mark in Table 1 and in the figure captions reads 'compared to Intact' or 'compared to placebo', so if all reported comparisons are strictly between groups at a single timepoint, the between-groups tests are appropriate at each timepoint and the issue reduces to unmodelled multiplicity across timepoints rather than a violated independence assumption. The before/after statements in the text are what prevent that benign reading from covering the whole paper.

consequence.explanation: Bears on Table 1 and on the four longitudinal figure outcomes -- rotarod, open field, and both Morris water maze series -- where the same animals are measured more than once.

findings.plain: The same rats were measured several times each -- at three hours, one day and ten days, and across four days of maze training. Comparing repeated measurements on the same animals needs a statistical method built for that; the paper lists only methods for comparing separate, independent groups. It may be that every comparison the authors actually report is between different groups at a single moment in time, in which case their methods are fine and the issue is smaller. But at least one sentence compares the same animals before and after treatment, and no method listed can produce that comparison.

findings.title: Cerebrolysin dose printed as 1641 mg/kg in two Results sentences against 1614 mg/kg throughout the rest of the paper
findings.location: Results 3.3.1 (chronic brain ischemia) and Results 3.4.3 (chronic brain ischemia); PDF page 9
findings.reported: "In the groups of animals with chronic brain ischemia treated with Cortexin at a dose of 1 mg/kg, Cerebrolysin at doses of 538 and 1641 mg/kg, as well as Actovegin, the performance on a rotating rod was statistically better than in the group receiving a placebo" (3.3.1); "The courses of Cortexin (1 and 3 mg/kg) and Cerebrolysin (538 and 1641 mg/kg) significantly increased motor activity" (3.4.3). The dose is 1614 mg/kg in the Abstract, Methods 2.12, the Table 1 row label, Results 3.5.2, Results 3.6.1, the Discussion and the Conclusions.
findings.computed: A digit transposition. No study arm at 1641 mg/kg exists in the design -- Methods 2.12 states "For Cerebrolysin the respective doses were 538 and 1614 mg/kg/day" and Table 1's row label reads "Cerebrolysin (1614 mg/kg)". Confirmed independently in both the XML and the PDF version of record, so it is a genuine error in the published text and not an extraction artefact.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Stated as an observation only; the intended arm is recoverable by any reader from the study design, so nothing numeric turns on it.

consequence.explanation: No claim changes: the intended arm is unambiguous from the study design, so this is a copy-editing defect in the published record rather than an analytic one.

findings.plain: Two sentences in the results give a drug dose of 1641 mg per kilogram; everywhere else in the paper -- the summary, the methods, the table, the discussion and the conclusion -- the dose is 1614. There was no 1641 group in the study, so this is a transposed pair of digits. A reader can work out what was meant, and no result depends on it, but it is an error in the published version of a drug dose.

findings.title: Discussion citation of a table of amino-acid mechanisms that the paper does not contain
findings.reported: "Also, the protective role of amino acids, the molecular mechanisms of which are listed in the table, cannot be ruled out."
findings.computed: No such table exists. The article contains exactly one table (Table 1, severity of neurological deficit by the Garcia and Combs & D'Alecy scales), confirmed by the XML table index (n_tables = 1). Neither supplementary file contains it either: S1 File is a table of group sizes and S2 File is a list of radioligand assay conditions across 28 assays. The sentence points at content that was never included.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own contents. Recorded descriptively; no inference is drawn about how it arose.

consequence.explanation: One Discussion claim about the protective mechanisms of amino acids is supported by a pointer to material absent from the article and its supplements.

findings.plain: The discussion tells the reader that the molecular mechanisms of certain amino acids are 'listed in the table'. There is no such table: the paper has one table, about neurological scores, and neither supplementary file contains the missing content. A supporting reference points at something that was never published with the paper.

findings.title: Morris water maze latencies right-censored at the 60-second trial cap and summarised as means
findings.location: Methods 2.6.5; Figs 7 and 8; Morris water maze trial columns of the linked figshare spreadsheet
findings.reported: Methods 2.6.5: "Each animal was placed in the apparatus 4 times for a maximum of 1 min ... If the rat did not find the platform for 1 min, it was placed on the platform and left for 15 s". Figs 7 and 8 caption: "data shown as the mean +/- SEM", analysed by "Kruskal-Wallis rank analysis and the Dunn post-hoc test".
findings.computed: In the deposited data file the value 60.0 -- the trial cutoff -- occurs 1,131 times across 12,201 numeric cells, and in individual water-maze entry columns it accounts for 120, 108, 95 and 61 rows apiece (columns '1st d - e', '2nd d - se', '1st d - se', '2nd d - n', counted by column name across the acute and chronic sheets, which together hold 187 animals). A large fraction of animals on the early training days therefore never found the platform and were assigned the ceiling value. A mean over a censored variable understates the true latency by an amount that depends on how many animals hit the cap, which differs by group and by day.
findings.assumptions: Left indeterminate deliberately. Right-censoring at the trial cap is intrinsic to the Morris water maze and summarising latency as mean +/- SEM is near-universal in this literature, so this is not a departure from field practice; the paper's inferential tests are rank-based and therefore partly robust to it. Whether it changes any conclusion cannot be determined without re-analysing the deposited data with a censoring-aware method, which no tool in this toolkit performs. Note also that the paper's own claim is confined to training days 2-4, where censoring is least severe, and it explicitly reports no group difference on day 1, where censoring is worst. Per-column tallies are the tool's occurrence counts and were not independently recounted.

consequence.explanation: Bears on how the size of the memory benefit in Figs 7 and 8 should be read, which carries the Abstract's claim of reduced cognitive impairment; whether the direction of any conclusion changes cannot be determined without re-analysis.

findings.plain: In the memory test, each rat had 60 seconds to find a hidden platform, and any rat that failed was simply recorded as 60. In the authors' own deposited data that 60-second value appears over a thousand times, accounting for a large share of animals on the first two days of training. Averaging such a measurement compresses the differences between groups toward the time limit, so the plotted averages understate how long some animals really would have taken. The authors' own significance tests are of a type that partly tolerates this, and their claim is limited to the later training days when fewer animals were hitting the limit -- so this is a caution about how large the memory benefit looks, not a demonstration that it is absent.

findings.title: Per-timepoint sample size behind the blood-brain-barrier claim unstated in the figure caption
findings.reported: Fig 13 caption: "Brain content of 125I-labeled Cortexin, Cerebrolysin and albumin in mice. Data shown as geometric mean (n = 15)." Methods 2.10: "In a separate experiment on male laboratory mice (n = 15 per group) ... after 0.5, 2 or 4 hours, animals (5 animals from each group) were killed by decapitation to determine the content of the radioactive label."
findings.computed: The sampling is destructive and 5 x 3 = 15 exactly, so each plotted timepoint necessarily rests on 5 mice, not 15. The caption's bare 'n = 15' is a correct statement of the group total but will read to most readers as the n behind each point. Whether that matters depends on how Fig 13 is laid out, and the figure was not read.
findings.assumptions: Left indeterminate because resolving it requires seeing the figure, which this review did not read. A caption stating the total group size is ordinary and legitimate practice; the concern is only that a reader may take it for the per-point n.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the precision behind the Abstract's claim that the drug crossed the blood-brain barrier at 6-8% of whole-blood concentrations, which derives from these timepoints.

findings.plain: A figure showing how much drug reached the brain over time is labelled 'n = 15'. But the methods explain that the mice had to be killed to take each measurement, five at each of three time points -- so each point on that graph rests on five animals, not fifteen. The label is defensible as a statement of the total group size, but a reader is likely to read it as three times more animals per measurement than there were, and the summary's headline figure about the drug reaching the brain comes from these points.

findings.title: Exact reconciliation of every stated sample size across four independent sources
findings.location: Methods 2.2, 2.3 and 2.10; Table 1 n column; S1 File Table A; linked figshare spreadsheet
findings.reported: Methods 2.2: "The study used 224 male albino rats". Methods 2.3: an additional experiment "in limited number of animals (n = 37) ... intact (n = 10), placebo (n = 9), 3 mg/kg Cortexin (n = 9), and 538 mg/kg Cerebrolysin (n = 9)". Methods 2.10: "n = 15 per group" with "5 animals from each group" killed at each of three timepoints. Fig 10 caption: "Brain necrosis volume at 3 days (n = 9)".
findings.computed: All four summation rows reconcile exactly at zero tolerance: the 18 group counts in S1 File sum to 224; the four 3-day groups sum to 37; 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 mice; and the Table 1 n column (15, 12, 12, 12, 12, 12, 12) sums to 87 and agrees cell-for-cell with the S1 File 10-day column. Fig 10's n = 9 also reconciles cleanly against S1 File once the intact group (n = 10, which contributes no infarct) is excluded from a necrosis comparison, leaving three surgical groups of 9 -- corroborated by the spreadsheet's 'Brain necrosis volume, %' column being blank for the intact rows. Table 1's XML extraction is structurally clean: not image-only, not alignment-uncertain, no warnings, and all four merged cells confined to the two-row header region.
findings.assumptions: Tolerance was set to zero because animal counts must hold exactly. This is the absence of a contradiction across the sample-size reporting, and it is a genuine strength; it does not verify any inferential claim.

consequence.explanation: Nothing is affected; this is a clean pass that raises confidence in the sample-size reporting specifically.

findings.plain: Everywhere the paper states how many animals were in a group, the numbers add up exactly -- the individual group sizes total the 224 rats claimed, the side-experiment's four groups total its stated 37, the mouse study's timepoints total 15, and the table's own column totals 87 and matches the supplement animal for animal. Sample-size bookkeeping is one thing this paper does carefully, and that is worth saying plainly.

not_checked.location: Figs 3-14: every quantitative outcome in the paper other than the Table 1 neurological scores
not_checked.reason: The group means, SEMs and per-point sample sizes behind Figs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14 are printed nowhere in the text, the table or the supplements -- they exist only as bars and lines. No figure-extraction pass was run in this review, and values read off pixels would in any case be barred from the exact-arithmetic checks. This is the single largest blind spot here: the seven-outcome antioxidant panel, both water-maze series, rotarod, open field, adhesive latency and hippocampal morphometry are all unchecked for this reason.

not_checked.location: Table 1 quartile granularity (Q1/Q3 printed as .3, .5, .8 for n = 12 and n = 15 integer-scale data)
not_checked.reason: The attainable-value set of a quartile of integer data at a given n is constrained, and the printed values suggest a specific interpolation convention. No validated tool in this toolkit checks median or quartile granularity -- GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require a mean and an SD. Deliberately not hand-derived, since unauditable arithmetic performed by the reviewer is exactly what a forensic check must not rest on.

not_checked.location: Linked figshare spreadsheet: cell-by-cell typed sweep of all 12,201 numeric cells
not_checked.reason: The file returns roughly 2.6 million characters across 124,730 lines, beyond what can be read without sampling, and a check built on a sampled table is worse than no check. The file was not left unswept: detect_raw_duplication loaded the entire grid across all 3 sheets, and its results were re-run and confirmed at this stage.

not_checked.location: Brain necrosis effect size (the 45% and 38% reductions, Results 3.7.1)
not_checked.reason: Only the placebo mean is printed (26 +/- 5%, n = 9); the Cortexin and Cerebrolysin group means are given only as relative reductions and their dispersions appear only in Fig 10. Computing an effect size would require deriving one group mean and inventing an SD, i.e. fabricating the tool's inputs.

The text gives only the placebo breakdown ("5 of 12 animals from placebo group did not find the duct tape, and 4 of 12 found it, but subsequently did not try to remove it"); the comparator counts appear only as percentages inside Fig 3, and no chi-squared statistic or degrees of freedom are reported for reconstruction.

GRIM-percentage was considered and deliberately not applied. These are percent inhibition of radioligand binding -- a continuous ratio, not a count out of a sample -- so the granularity argument does not hold and running the test would manufacture a false impossibility.

not_checked.location: All p-values in the paper, for rank-sum granularity (GRIM-U)
not_checked.reason: Not applicable on two independent grounds: the paper uses Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn post-hoc, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni t-tests, and chi-squared -- none of which is a Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon rank-sum test -- and it reports no exact p-values in any case.

not_checked.location: Baseline similarity across treatment groups (Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher and Table 1 dispersion)
not_checked.reason: No baseline table exists and neither test has the inputs it requires. Table 1's 3-hour column is a post-ischemia severity measure rather than a pre-randomisation baseline, it is reported as median/IQR rather than mean/SD/n, and no baseline p-values are printed anywhere. No baseline-uniformity claim is made or contradicted in this review.

Could not be run: the paper states no power calculation, no target power, no assumed effect size and no sample-size justification. Group sizes of 12-15 across seven arms are asserted without rationale. The absence is itself a reporting observation.

Not applicable: the paper contains exactly one table and its cells are median [Q1;Q3], not the (mean, SD) pairs the duplication check compares. Several Table 1 cells are identical across groups (for example '4 [3;4]' in four treatment rows of the Combs 3 h column), but on a 9-point integer scale at n = 12 with near-identical post-ischemia severity, identical medians and IQRs are the expected result of a tight bounded distribution.

not_checked.location: S2 File in vitro binding assay table (28 rows x 7 columns)
not_checked.reason: Swept and found to contain no checkable statistics. Every cell is a protocol parameter -- assay source, radioligand, ligand concentration, Kd, non-specific binding compound, incubation time -- not a study result.

Not present in the extracted XML body and therefore not assessed. Noted because the paper's conclusions favour a specific commercial product and the Discussion names its manufacturer ("Cortexin is produced by the pharmaceutical company Geropharm"), so a reader would want the sponsorship and affiliation record alongside these results.

not_checked.location: Reference [11] (Tyurenkov et al. 2020), from which some chronic-series data are explicitly republished
not_checked.reason: The paper twice discloses that chronic-series water maze and morphometry data "was partially shown earlier [11]". That disclosure is good practice, but this review reaches no network and could not retrieve the earlier paper, so the extent of overlap and whether the two reports are mutually consistent were not assessed. Readers should not treat the chronic-series cognitive and morphometric results as an independent replication.

limitations: FIGURES WERE NOT READ. This agent reads text and tables; no figure-extraction pass was run on this paper, and nothing in this review rests on a value read off a chart. That matters unusually much here, because every quantitative outcome except the Table 1 neurological scores exists only as a bar or line in Figs 3-14, with the underlying means, SEMs and per-point sample sizes printed nowhere in the text, the table or the supplements. A large majority of this paper's numeric content was therefore outside the reach of this review by construction.

No finding reached `impossible` or `highly_suspicious`, so no R cross-check against `scrutiny` or `rsprite2` was required, and none was run. Nothing in this report claims a mathematical impossibility.

Two of the four questions a duplication or similarity result must be read against are outside this system's reach entirely: it reads one paper and reaches no network, so it cannot say whether similar patterns appear in other papers by these authors -- including reference [11], from which some chronic-series data are explicitly republished -- or how these values compare with equivalent studies of Cortexin, Cerebrolysin and Actovegin. Those parts of the interpretation belong to the reader.

`check_sd_or_se` raised a TypeError when passed the printed precision of the value and had to be re-run without it, so its plausibility ceiling used a flat 1% margin rather than the value's actual precision. This is a defect in our tooling, not in the paper, and it is the reason that check is reported as discarded rather than as a finding.

Table 1 admits no arithmetic verification of any kind: all 49 cells are median [Q1;Q3] on ordinal scales plus a bare count column, and every granularity test in this toolkit requires a mean and a standard deviation. The paper's only table is arithmetically unfalsifiable, so `consistent` is not available for it in either direction -- absence of a contradiction there is not verification.

The verdict of `questionable` rests on a specific, nameable unresolved matter rather than on caution: the paper's principal claims -- that Cortexin and Cerebrolysin are comparably effective, and that both reduce cognitive and sensorimotor impairment -- could not be checked, because no drug-versus-drug test is reported and no inferential statistic anywhere in the paper is recomputable from what is printed.

The per-column tallies of the 60-second water-maze ceiling are the duplication tool's own occurrence counts, matched by column name across sheets rather than within a single experiment; they were not independently recounted, and the exact per-column denominators were not verified.

questions_for_authors.question: The Conclusions state that "Cortexin (1 or 3 mg/kg) as well as Cerebrolysin (538 or 1614 mg/kg) were comparable effective", but every reference mark in Table 1 and in the captions of Figs 3-12 reads either "compared to Intact" or "compared to placebo". Which specific statistical comparison between the Cortexin and Cerebrolysin arms supports the comparability claim, and what were its test statistic and p-value?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether a head-to-head analysis exists and was simply not reported, or whether the comparative conclusion is inferred from separate placebo comparisons. This is the paper's headline claim.

questions_for_authors.question: Results 3.6.1 states: "In animals treated with Cerebrolysin at a dose of 1614 mg/kg/day, most of the indicators were comparable to those obtained in animals treated with Cortexin at a dose of 3 mg/kg/day (p <0.05)." Two sentences earlier the same paragraph uses "p> 0.05 in each case" for a no-difference statement. Should the p-value in the first sentence read p>0.05, or is a difference rather than comparability intended?
questions_for_authors.why: This is the only place in the paper where a p-value is attached to a Cortexin-versus-Cerebrolysin comparison, and as printed it points the opposite way from the claim it supports.

questions_for_authors.question: Were the Garcia and Combs & D'Alecy scores, the behavioural tests and the morphometric classification of neurons recorded by an assessor unaware of each animal's group allocation? And by what method were animals allocated to groups in the 87-animal acute series and the 100-animal chronic series -- the word "randomly" appears in the paper only for the 37-animal sub-experiment.
questions_for_authors.why: The primary and morphological outcomes are observer-rated and therefore expectancy-sensitive; blinding and allocation are not reported for the two main series, and the article's own limitations paragraph does not address them.

questions_for_authors.question: Methods 2.2 states "The study used 224 male albino rats", and the 18 group counts in S1 File sum to exactly 224, leaving no animals unaccounted for. Were any animals lost to surgical mortality, died during follow-up, or were excluded from analysis, and if so how many from each group? Relatedly, is 224 the number obtained or the number analysed?
questions_for_authors.why: 184 of the 224 animals underwent ischemia surgery, including 87 given 90-minute filament middle cerebral artery occlusion, and no deaths, exclusions or attrition are reported anywhere. The uneven chronic-series group sizes (15, 13, 15, 14, 15, 13, 15) would be consistent with unreported losses.

questions_for_authors.question: Results 3.3.1 and 3.4.3 give a Cerebrolysin dose of "538 and 1641 mg/kg", while Methods 2.12, the Table 1 row label, the Abstract, the Discussion and the Conclusions all give 1614 mg/kg. Which is correct? Separately, the Discussion states that the molecular mechanisms of amino acids "are listed in the table" -- which table is intended, given that the article contains only Table 1 (neurological deficit scores) and neither supplementary file lists such mechanisms?
questions_for_authors.why: Two errors in the published record: a transposed drug dose in two efficacy sentences, and a citation pointing at material absent from the article and its supplements. Both are correctable and neither is recoverable from the text alone.

questions_for_authors.question: Fig 14 reports receptor binding as "median and range (n = 2)", while S2 File documents a 28-assay panel and the text names five targets (AMPA 80.1%, kainate 73.5%, mGluR1 49.0%, GABAA1 44.0%, mGluR5 39.7%). Are the individual duplicate values for each assay available, and does Fig 14 display all 28 assayed targets or only a subset?
questions_for_authors.why: The Abstract's and Conclusions' mechanistic claim rests on duplicate assays reported to one decimal place, and a reader cannot currently see how the five highlighted targets compare with the other 23.

input.report_markdown:
This paper compares three polypeptide preparations used clinically in Russia and several post-Soviet states -- Cortexin, Cerebrolysin and Actovegin -- in rat models of acute (middle cerebral artery occlusion) and chronic (bilateral carotid stenosis) brain ischemia, across 224 rats in three series, supported by a mouse biodistribution study and an in vitro receptor panel. It concludes that Cortexin and Cerebrolysin were comparably effective, that Actovegin was inferior to both, and that Cortexin crosses the blood-brain barrier and binds glutamatergic and GABAergic receptors.

The defect that matters here is not arithmetic. It is that the paper's central claim is a comparison it never performed. The stated aim is a head-to-head evaluation, and the Conclusions deliver one -- but every test reported carries one of exactly two reference marks, "compared to Intact" or "compared to placebo", and those two marks are repeated verbatim through Table 1's footnotes and the captions of Figs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12. Two drugs each beating a placebo does not establish that they match each other, and since no confidence interval appears anywhere in the paper, the largest true difference between them that the data still permit cannot be bounded. The same structure supports the claim that Actovegin is inferior: it is inferred from Actovegin failing to reach significance against placebo where the others reached it, which is a statement about two tests, not about the difference between two drugs.

Everything else in the review follows from a second, related fact. The paper reports roughly thirty significance claims and, for every one, prints only a threshold. No test statistic, no degrees of freedom, no exact p-value, no effect size, no interval -- statcheck recovers zero statistics from the whole article, which is an accurate description of the reporting rather than a tool failure. The multiplicity arithmetic likewise returns zero evaluable tests: all fourteen Table 1 comparisons are bounds and were dropped rather than coerced, so no correction can be computed. To be fair on that last point, this is not uncorrected testing -- Dunn's post-hoc and the stated Bonferroni correction do control multiplicity. The problem is that neither can be verified.

Two things pull in the paper's favour and deserve saying without hedging. First, the sample-size bookkeeping is exact. The eighteen group counts sum to the stated 224 with zero slack; the sub-experiment's four groups sum to its stated 37; the mouse timepoints sum to 15; Table 1's n column sums to 87 and matches the supplement animal for animal; and Fig 10's n = 9 reconciles once the intact group, which contributes no infarct, is excluded. Second, the data availability statement is honoured. The linked figshare deposit exists, loads, and contains participant-level data across three sheets and 12,201 numeric cells -- the opposite of the state-but-withhold pattern. That materially softens the reporting blackout: the article cannot be checked, but the evidence behind it can be re-analysed by anyone willing to start over.

Three sweep flags did not survive triage and are recorded here rather than published as findings. The repeated quarter-fraction values in the deposited spreadsheet (33.75, 32.25, 37.75 and thirty-one others) are not duplication: every flagged value ends in .25, .5 or .75, and every flagged column sits at a stride of five -- four daily water-maze trials plus their average. Averaging four integer-second latencies produces multiples of 0.25 by construction, so the apparent four-digit precision is an artefact of dividing by four. The one flagged duplicated row pair is dominated by the 60-second maze ceiling and small integers on bounded scales, matches on only twenty of roughly forty-five columns -- a genuine copy would match on all of them -- and its own "2nd d average search time" match is arithmetically determined by the four trial values in the same row, so it is not independent evidence. And the placebo necrosis volume of 26 +/- 5% was flagged as a possible standard-deviation/standard-error confusion; it is not one. Methods 2.13 and the Fig 10 caption both state the SEM convention explicitly, and under that reading the implied standard deviation of 15 (a coefficient of variation near 58%) is entirely ordinary for filament MCAO infarct volume, whereas the tool's preferred reading would make it implausibly tight. The heuristic points the wrong way there. The duplicated section number 3.3.1 was likewise set aside as pure copy-editing with no numeric consequence.

What remains is a study whose bookkeeping is careful, whose data are genuinely shared, and whose printed inferential content cannot be checked at any point -- reporting its main comparison as a conclusion rather than as an analysis, and scoring its principal outcomes by human observers whose blinding is never stated.

I do not think the reported statistics can be verified from this article, and the comparative conclusion it leads with is not supported by any analysis it reports; the deposited raw data are the reason this is a call for re-analysis rather than a dismissal.
